The Hebrew word JALIN (ילין), for which the Seventy translated slept, means both rested and will rest, that is, it signifies both the past and the future tense. Hence Aquila and Theodotion too speak as of the future. And he marvels in the prophetic spirit that the city which was once faithful, or the dwelling of the faithful, has suddenly become a harlot. …
1:22:
58. He denounces the sin of the priest in two matters.

In corrupting the truth of doctrine: hence he says, your silver is turned into dross: the words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times (Ps 11:7[12:6]). The prophets prophesied falsehood (Jer 5:31).

 …

Your silver is turned into dross. He speaks to the city of Zion, in which righteousness formerly rested: that its silver, namely the teaching of the Scriptures, of which we read in the Psalms, The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved in the earth, refined sevenfold (Ps 11 [12]:7), is turned into dross, which in Hebrew is called SIGIM (סיגים): namely the rust of metals, or the refuse and filth that are smelted out by fire; so that, since he had named silver, he keeps the metaphor. …
1:23:
59. Your princes are faithless. Here he denounces the sin of the princes.

And first, he shows that they are unfaithful in executing their office, because they do so for their own advantage and not that of the people: that anoint themselves with the best ointments, that drink wine in bowls (Amos 6:6); woe to the shepherds of Israel, that feed themselves: should not the flocks be fed by the shepherds? (Ezek 34:2); and because of this, he says they are faithless.

 …

Your princes are disobedient, companions of thieves. For disobedient, Aquila translated withdrawing, Symmachus turning aside. And by princes he means the Scribes and Pharisees, who, withdrawing from the Lord, or rather leaving the path of truth, walked on a perverse road and were companions of Judas, the betrayer and thief. …
1:24:
60. Therefore says the Lord. Here he threatens punishment:

and first, the punishment of the superiors;

second, of the subjects, where it says, and I will turn my hand to you (Isa 1:25).

Concerning the first, he sets out three things.

First, the power of the one who punishes in authority, saying, the Lord: if I be a master, where is my fear, says the Lord (Mal 1:6); in the multitude of his ministers: the God of hosts: is there any numbering of his soldiers? …

Therefore says the Lord of hosts, the mighty one of Israel. For the mighty one of Israel, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone, intending I know not what, put: Woe, you mighty of Israel; which we can expound thus, by saying that the princes too and the strong are rebuked, of whom it is written: The mighty shall mightily suffer torments (Wis 6:7); and: To whom more is given, more will be required of him (Luke 12:48). …
1:26: And I will restore your judges as they were before, and your counselors as of old. In the faithful city of Zion, which afterwards became a harlot, murderers dwelt in place of the righteous one, or of righteousness. Therefore the Lord turns his hand, to smelt her to purity and take away all her tin, and to restore her judges as they were at the beginning, and her counselors as of old. …
1:27: Zion shall be redeemed, from oppressors, in judgment, through the execution of justice; and they shall bring her back in justice, because judgment is the restoration of the equality in which justice consists: to judge your people with justice, and your poor with judgment (Ps 71[72]:2); a king shall reign and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth (Jer 23:5).

Zion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back into righteousness, and he shall crush the wicked and the sinners together; and those who have forsaken the Lord shall be consumed; for they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed, and you shall blush over the gardens which you had chosen. Not all will be redeemed, nor will all be saved, but the remnant, of whom it was spoken above too. …
1:28: Moreover, who can agree with the thesis that you [the Pelagians] set down as your next heading: "In the day of judgment, no leniency shall be shown to the ungodly and to sinners, but they shall be consumed in eternal fires," for you prevent God from showing mercy, and you pass judgment on the sentence of the judge before judgment day, so that if he wanted to spare the unjust and the sinner, he could not, in view of your prescription? …
1:30:
65. When you shall be. Here he places the subtraction of good.

And first, of that which pertains to protection and adornment, which is signified by the removal of leaves; second, of that which pertains to fruit, where it says, as a garden, which is barren without water. And on the contrary, it is said of the just man: he shall be like a tree which is planted near the running waters (Ps 1:3).

For they shall be like a terebinth whose leaves fall off, and like a garden, or a paradise, without water. To this day the Jews, reading the holy Scriptures, are a terebinth, or an oak, as Symmachus translated. And according to the Gospel (Matt 21) they are the fig tree that withered, on which the Lord sought fruit and, not finding it, cursed it with everlasting barrenness. …
1:31:
66. And your strength shall be. Here he takes away from them the hope of escape; and he sets out three things.

First, he takes away the support of their own strength; hence he says, your strength shall be as the ashes of tow, which are quickly consumed: the congregation of sinners is like tow heaped together (Sir 21:10[9]).

Second, he takes away the help of idols, saying: your work, namely, of idols, which were made by your hands, as a spark, which is of no importance: where are their gods, in whom they trusted? …

And your strength shall be like the ash of tow. For ash, Symmachus translated ἀποτίναγμα: when tow is combed, and whatever filth it has is thrown away. So all the strength and pride of the sinners and wicked of Israel, who forsook the Lord and were therefore consumed, and sacrificed to idols, and will blush in the gardens which they chose, will be reduced to the refuse of tow, which is devoured by a light fire. …
1:4:
33. He adds to the weight of the effect of the deed, however, through its confirmed use:

hence he first shows the confirmation,

and second, shows their turning away: they have forsaken the Lord.

He shows the confirmation first through the custom of sin, which gives rise to habit: hence he says, the sinful nation; for a sinner is such out of habit just as a singer is such out of art or office, below: I have called you a transgressor from the womb (Isa 48:8).

 …

Woe to the sinful nation, to a people heavy with iniquity, to a wicked seed, to criminal sons: they have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, they are estranged backward. What I have put last, they are estranged backward, the Seventy Translators do not have; and for they have blasphemed there is written in them, they have provoked to anger; and for a wicked seed, a most evil seed. …
1:6: 36. Third, where it says, wounds and bruises, he removes the manner of correction which is through human exertion, as when someone is disposed to grace, which blots out sins through good works. Hence he says, wounds, open fault, and bruises, hidden envy, and swelling sores, inflating pride, they are not bound up, by the bond of the law drawing them back: of old time you have broken my yoke, you have burst my bands, and you said: I will not serve (Jer 2:20), as to the first; nor dressed, with healing charity, as to …

It is not bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor soothed with oil. For which the Seventy translated: It is not possible to apply a plaster, nor oil, nor bandages. To this day the wound and bruise and swelling sore of the people of Israel is not bound up with bandages, nor treated with medicine. Which Aquila translated μότωσιν, namely the lint which is laid on wounds to dry up the matter and draw out the pus. Nor soothed with oil: that their hardness might be softened by tears of repentance. …
1:8: Third, as to the captivity of men: hence he says, the daughter of Zion shall be left, that is, Jerusalem or the temple, from which came the protection of the whole province, as it was solitary and as a covert in a vineyard after the harvest, below: for the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel: and the man of Judah, his pleasant plant (Isa 5:7); as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, after the last fruits have been collected, through which he signifies their fathers: I saw their fathers like the first …

The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field. That all Israel is called a vineyard the same Prophet testifies in what follows, saying: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his young and beloved planting (below, Isa 5:7); and in the Psalm: You have brought a vine out of Egypt; you have cast out the nations and planted it (Ps 79 [80]:9). …
20:1:
In the year that. Here the time of destruction is set out, and it is divided into three parts. And first is set out something that signifies, namely a prophetic deed; second, the signification of the deed: and the Lord said (Isa 20:3); third, he shows the effect of the thing signified: and they shall be afraid, and confounded (Isa 20:5).

Concerning the first, he does three things. …

In the year that Tartan came into Ashdod, when Sargon the king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Ashdod and had taken it, at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying: Go, and loose the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoes off your feet. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot. And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent of three years upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia. …
20:2:
Second, he sets out the divine command: go, and loose: and Ezechiel shall be unto you for a sign of things to come (Ezek 24:24).

Third, the fulfillment of the command: and he did so, below: and I do not resist (Isa 50:5).

At the time, then, when the neighboring city was taken, Isaiah is commanded to lay aside his tunic of sackcloth (for this was the garb of the prophet lamenting the sins of the people), and the shoes from his feet, which the Seventy call caligae, and to go about naked and barefoot, presenting a type of the captivity of the Egyptians and of the Ethiopians, who had been a help to the Egyptians: that just as Isaiah walked naked and displayed his unsightliness to the onlookers with bare buttocks, so all Egypt and …
20:3:
And the Lord said. Here the signification of the aforementioned deed is set out.

And first, as to the time for which the persecution lasted: three years, signified by the three days in which he went naked: a day for a year I have appointed to you (Ezek 4:6).
And when it is said: A sign and portent of three years will be upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia, this signifies that Egypt and Ethiopia were to be laid waste by the Assyrians for three years.
20:4:
Second, as to the author of the destruction: so shall the king be led: in that day shall messengers go forth from my face in ships to destroy the confidence of Ethiopia (Ezek 30:9).

Third, as to the condition of the destruction, into universality: young and old; into baseness: naked, namely, captivity: there is no cure for you (Jer 46:11).

And in that very captivity and exile of Egypt shall go the young and the old, who have been hardened in wickedness and have come to the vices of full age: naked, so that all their crimes may be laid bare (for nothing (Luke 8:17) is hidden that shall not be revealed), and barefoot, because they will not be able to eat the Passover of the Lord; for whoever eats it has his loins girded, and holds a staff in his hand, and stands with shod feet, lest, passing through the wilderness of this world, he be bitten by …
20:5: And they shall be afraid. Here he places the effect on the Jews; first, fear, and they shall be afraid; second, confusion, and confounded.

Then, he says, the inhabitant of this island will say, that is, Jerusalem, which is beaten by the waves of the neighboring nations: Was this our hope? And did we flee to these to give us help, who could not rescue themselves from the evil of captivity? This, then, is the order of the providence of God, who disposes the whole race of men by his ineffable judgment. Against the wrath of God Israel hoped in Damascus: let the city be destroyed which, against his will, gives help to the impious. …
20:6:
Third, the expression of both of these effects: and the inhabitants of this isle, that is, Jerusalem, which was incessantly beaten by waves of persecution, like an isle beaten by the waves of the sea.

Lo this was our hope, in which their confusion is expressed, and how shall we be able to escape, in which their fear is expressed, below: the strength of Pharaoh shall be to your confusion (Isa 30:3).
21:1: And rightly, according to the Hebrew, whirlwinds and tempests come from the desert and from a terrible land, where God is not the inhabitant, and where all things are earthly; and whoever is unbelieving does a thing in keeping with his faithlessness, and he who is a spoiler lays waste. Hence he speaks boldly against his adversaries: Go up, Elam; besiege, O Mede: I have made all the groaning of the desert of the sea, and of the terrible land, and of the hardest vision that has been told, to cease. …
21:10: 518. Fourth, the declaration of the prophet to the people is set out: O my thrashing, the words of the prophet, or of Christ, that Jerusalem is to be thrashed with many tribulations, children of my floor, that is, the temple, which is located on the thrashing floor of Ornam (2 Sam 24:18); whatsoever thing he shall answer me, I will declare it to you (Jer 42:4).

28:26: Second, the discretion of his judgment, for he punishes some in one way and others in a different way, just as a farmer beats out wheat in one way and cumin in another, and he indicates this where it says: for he will instruct him in judgment. Bread, that is, grain.
And God by his judgment instructs the farmer himself, that is, the sower, by nature, and teaches him to know what cultivation to apply to which seed.
28:28: Third, the ending of punishments as to those who are corrected: but the thrasher shall not thrash it for ever: he that ploughs, should plough in hope, and he that thrashes, in hope to receive fruit (1 Cor 9:10).

And that passage in which we, according to the Hebrew, have put: Yet the thresher shall not thresh it forever, nor shall the wheel of the cart vex it, nor shall he crush it with its hoofs, the Seventy translated not word for word but according to the sense: For I will not be angry with you forever, nor shall the voice of my bitterness trample you down: showing that refreshment is to come to sinners after torments, and that these things have gone forth from the Lord as portents and wonders. …
28:29: Third, he sets out the explanation: this also is come forth from the Lord God of hosts, to make his counsel wonderful: wonderful are your works (Ps 134[135]:14).

But this, that is, that gith and cumin are beaten out with a rod and a staff, while wheat and barley and spelt, and perhaps millet too, are ground by iron wheels, not forever, is the judgment of God, who in all things shows his wonderful counsel and displays the greatness of his righteousness in all. These things we have said παραφραστικῶς, so that we may more easily understand the sense for which they are said.
28:3: Second, he sets out the inflicting of the punishment, namely, the casting down of pride: the crown of pride shall be trodden under feet: in your anger you will tread the earth under foot (Hab 3:12).
28:4: And the emptying of glory, and the flower shall be as a hasty fruit, that is, ripe or early fruit, above: for before the harvest it was all flourishing (Isa 18:5); all your strong holds shall be like fig trees with their green figs (Nah 3:12).
28:5: 636. Third, he sets out the glory of the just, namely, of the just of the two tribes: in that day, namely, in the time of Ezechias, when the ten tribes had been destroyed; as to three things. As to the joy of the people, a crown, which is of gold or silver, in contrast to the crown of pride; a garland, of flowers, in contrast to the fading flower, below: and I will give them a crown for ashes (Isa 61:3).

In that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of judgment to him who sits upon judgment, and strength to those returning from war to the gate. …
28:6: As to the justice of the king: and he, the Lord himself, shall be a spirit of judgment: a king shall reign, and shall be wise: and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth (Jer 23:5). As to the might of their soldiers: and strength, for the Lord will fight for them, above: because you have been my strength (Isa 25:4).
28:7: 637. But these also. Here he threatens against those among the two tribes who disdain the predictions of the prophets; and first, against the princes, second, against the city or against the people, woe to Ariel (ch. 29). The first of these is divided into two parts. First, he sets out the threat; second, the consolation: give ear (Isa 28:23). Concerning the first, he does two things. …
28:8: Third, he sets out the manner of their ignorance: for all the tables were full of vomit, for they gorged themselves in their temples until they vomited, as if they were devoted entirely to idols; and filth, namely, of all their shameful vices: as a dog that returns to his vomit (Prov 26:11), and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

According to the anagogy, that Hebrew text in which we said: For all their tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no more room, can be referred to the heretics, and to the scribes and Pharisees, in this way: that we say all their teaching and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth, since they do not digest the food of the holy Scriptures nor make it life-giving to the whole body, but void it unripe and stinking, so that God finds no place in them. …
28:9: 639. Second, he threatens the punishment of blindness: whom shall he teach? Hence the question is first set out, whom shall he teach knowledge? As if to say: why have you spurned knowledge? The hearing, namely, what I heard from the Lord. …

Whom shall he teach knowledge, and whom shall he make to understand what is heard? Those weaned from the milk, those drawn from the breasts: for command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there. For with speech of lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said: This is my rest; refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment, and they would not hear. …
29:1: 651. Woe to Ariel. In this part, he sets out threatening against the people or against the city, and this is divided into two parts; in the first, he threatens the punishment of temporal destruction; in the second, the punishment of spiritual blinding: be astonished (Isa 29:9). Concerning the first, he does two things: in the first, he threatens destruction; in the second, he sets out consolation of any kind: and the multitude of all nations that have fought against Ariel, shall be as the dream (Isa 29:7). …

At the beginning of this chapter too, where we have said: Year has been added to year, or taken away, they translated: gather the fruits, or produce, year upon year: eat, for you shall eat with Moab. And the sense is: before the acceptable year of the Lord, of his preaching, comes, or rather the two years, of which we read in the Canticle of Habakkuk according to the Hebrew: In the midst of two times you shall be known (Hab 3), sow for yourselves in tears, that you may reap in joy (Ps 125 [126]). …
29:10: Second, he sets out the manner of blinding: for the Lord has mingled for you the spirit of a deep sleep, that is, as if he offered mixed wine to drink; he will shut up your eyes, namely, the prophets, above: the Lord has mingled in the midst thereof the spirit of giddiness (Isa 19:14).
29:11: Third, he sets out the effect of the blinding, for they will not understand the book of the Sacred Scriptures and the visions of all the prophets: and the vision of all shall be unto you as the words of a book that is sealed: and I saw, in the right hand of him that sat on the throne, a book, sealed with seven seals (Rev 5:1).

In the Apocalypse a book is shown sealed with seven seals, which if you deliver to one that is learned saying, "Read this," he will answer you, "I cannot, for it is sealed." How many there are today who fancy themselves learned, yet the Scriptures are a sealed book to them, and one which they cannot open save through him who has the key of David, "he that opens and no man shuts; and shuts and no man opens." In the Acts of the Apostles the holy eunuch when reading Isaiah is asked by Philip, "Do you understand what …
29:15: 661. Woe to you that are deep of heart. Here he sets out their sin on the part of the intellect, for they did not believe in the providence of God, that he knew what happens among us. And concerning this, he does two things. First, the devising of error is set out, and they said this was hidden from God because of the depth of their heart, where they handled their wicked counsels; hence he says: woe to you that are deep of heart: the heart is deep above all things, and unsearchable, who can know it? …

Woe to you who are deep of heart, to hide counsel from the Lord, whose works are in darkness, and they say: Who sees us, and who knows us? This thought of yours is perverse, as if the clay should think against the potter, and the work say to its maker: You did not make me; and the thing formed say to him who formed it: You do not understand. LXX: Woe to those who make deep counsel, and their works shall be in darkness, and they say: Who sees us? who shall know us, and what we are doing? …
29:17:
663. Is it not yet a very little while? Here he foretells the conversion of the gentiles, and concerning this, he does three things. First, he foretells their conversion to grace: Libanus, a gentile people, for the mountain was in the land of the gentiles; into Carmel, into grace, which the Jews had through circumcision, because Carmel means "knowledge of circumcision"; as a forest, that is, as barrenness, which the gentiles were in before, below (Isa 32:15) has the same thing.

666. …

Is it not yet a little while, and a short time, and Lebanon shall be turned into Charmel, and Charmel shall be reckoned as a forest? And in that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see. And the meek shall increase their joy in the Lord, and the poor among men shall exult in the Holy One of Israel: for he who prevailed has failed. …
29:18: To sacred knowledge: the deaf, namely, the gentiles, who had not heard the words of the law before: the blind see (Matt 11:5); for judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind (John 9:39).

When Lebanon has been changed into Charmel, and Charmel into a forest, then those who before were deaf and could not hear the words of the prophetic book (of which we said above that all holy Scripture is called one book, as the Preacher says (Eccl 12:11): The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fixed deep, which are given from the councils by one shepherd) shall hear, and shall speak, those to whom the Savior will say: Ephphetha, which means be opened (Mark 7). …
29:19: To spiritual joy: and the meek shall increase their joy: I will be glad, and rejoice in you: I will sing to your name, O you Most High (Ps 9:3[2]).

When those who were before blind have either beheld all the mystical things, or have lifted their eyes from blindness and darkness to see, so that the true light may rise for those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death: then the meek, of whom it is written: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth (Matt 5:4); or the poor, whose prince says in the psalms: This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him (Ps 33 [34]:7); and: who shall judge the poor of the people, and shall save the sons of the poor …
29:2:
The siege: and I will make a trench, namely, by the Chaldees: and lay siege against it (Ezek 4:2); and he intimates the taking of the city from its sadness: and it shall be in sorrow: my sighs are many (Lam 1:22).

654. Third, he sets out the reparation made under Jesus the high priest and others, about whom it is written through all of Ezra. And it shall be to me as Ariel, as if to say: retaining a shadow of its former dignity. …

And the Lord says that he will surround Ariel with a rampart, with the Babylonian army, and that it will be sad and mourning when it has been destroyed by them. And again, under Jeshua son of Jozadak the high priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and Ezra and Nehemiah, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, it will be like Ariel, in that it will have the likeness of the ancient temple, but not have its magnificence and adornment.
29:20: 664. Second, he indicates the occasion or the reason of their conversion: from the fall of the devil: for he that did prevail, by power, has failed, the scorner, the deceiver by cunning, above: the wretch is consumed: he has failed, that trod the earth under foot (Isa 16:4); from the blindness of the Jewish people, that blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in (Rom 11:25). …

And there is every exultation, because he who prevailed has failed. The scorner is consumed, or the arrogant and proud one, who had said: By strength I will do it, and by wisdom; I will remove the bounds of the nations and lay waste their strength; who mocked all, so much so that the saint too said: My loins are filled with illusions (Ps 37 [38]:8). …
29:21: That made men sin, by wicked example and teaching; that reproved them in the gate, as to contempt of instruction: they have hated him that rebukes in the gate (Amos 5:10); and declined in vain from the just, as to the vanity of sin, for that is vain, which fails to attain its end: what has pride profited us? Or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us? (Wis 5:8).
29:22: 665. Third, he sets out the conversion of the Jews at the end of the world, when he says: therefore thus says the Lord that redeemed Abraham, Genesis 11; Jacob shall not now, that is, at this time, be confounded, by a good confounding: there is a confounding that brings glory and grace (Sir 4:25).

Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham: Jacob shall not now be confounded, nor shall his face now blush: but when he sees his sons, the works of my hands, in his midst sanctifying my name: and they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall proclaim the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit shall know understanding, and the mutterers shall learn the Law. …
29:23:
His children, the Apostles.

666. Or this may be otherwise explained as concerning the prosperity that was promised to them when Sennacherib or Nabuchodonosor were destroyed: he shall see his children . . . sanctifying my name (Isa 29:23), the three children in the furnace of fire; or that their children will praise my name, because they themselves in their youth did not.
29:24: They that murmured, that is, who at first murmured, above: when they shall rush out from Jacob, Israel shall blossom (Isa 27:6).
29:3: 655. And I will encircle. Here he threatens destruction by the Romans. And concerning this, he sets out four things. First, the siege: and I will encircle you like a sphere, that is, round about: your enemies shall cast a trench about you (Luke 19:43); he shall laugh at every strong hold, and shall cast up a mount (Hab 1:10).

A second time also the Lord threatens that he will surround Ariel with a ring, and cast up a mound against it, and set up fortifications for its siege, and that what he himself says, lamenting Jerusalem in the Gospel, will be fulfilled: If you knew the things that are for your peace, for days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, and besiege you, and you shall be brought low to the ground (Luke 19:42ff.). …
29:4: Second, the humiliation of the besieged: you shall be humbled; and the sign of their humiliation, you shall speak out of the earth, that is, just as if you were under the earth, so shall you humbly be heard, bearing the words of the python, which chanted silently: I will take away out of the midst of you your proud boasters (Zeph 3:11); or their meriting of humiliation, accusing them of the sin of avarice: you shall speak out of the earth, and idolatry: and your voice shall be like that of the python.

For in other words the prophet now says the same thing: that, brought low, it speaks from the earth, and its speech is heard from the ground; and its voice is like that of a python from the earth, and from the ground it mutters like sparrows; so that by these words he signifies the νεκυομαντείαν of the magicians, by which they are said to call up souls and to hear the thin voices of shades, or rather of demons. …
29:5: Third, he sets out the multitude of the enemy: and the multitude of them that fan you, shall be like small dust: a nation come up upon my land (Joel 1:6), or the destruction of the enemy, as above: he shall be carried away as the dust of the mountains before the wind (Isa 17:13).

And so great an army of Roman power will encompass you, O Ariel, that it will be compared to countless dust, like ash flying through the air. Hence he compares to dust and ash not the weakness of those who made war against them, but their multitude, which is equal to the countless sands.
29:6: Fourth, he sets out the destruction itself: and it shall be at an instant suddenly, metaphorically, because of the ferocity of the enemy: he shall come up as a cloud, and his chariots as a tempest: his horses are swifter than eagles (Jer 4:13).

And this will be suddenly, at once, so that in the midst of peace sudden wars arise under Nero, and the Lord of hosts visits Jerusalem with thunder, and with the shaking of the earth, and with the whirlwind of tempest, and with the flame of devouring fire, by which he signifies that the temple was to be burned.
29:7: 656. And the multitude of all nations that have fought against Ariel, shall be as the dream. Here he adds some consolation from the punishment of the enemy, for like a vain thing, they will go into nothing, not carrying back anything advantageous from the destruction of Judea, just as someone hungry or thirsty gets nothing from food or drink he dreams of: the hopes of a man that is void of understanding are vain and deceitful: and dreams lift up fools (Sir 34:1); I will make Jerusalem a burdensome stone to all …

And the Romans, who, when the Jews had been overcome and Jerusalem overthrown under Titus and Vespasian, offered to the Capitol spoils from the vessels that once were God's, and thought that what they had done was the work of their own valor and of the power of their gods, not of the wrath of God, will possess all their riches as in a dream and in a vision of the night. …
2:10: Second, he places, ironically, the counsel to escape, saying, "enter you"; as if to say, since he himself does not send you away, it remains that you should hide yourself from his face. "Enter you into the rock," literally, into the fissures of the rocks to remain there; "hide you in the pit," that is, in the caverns of the earth, "from the face of the fear of the Lord," that is, from the face of those through whom God proves that he is to be feared and glorified: "leave the cities" (Jer 48:28); but this does not …

Enter into the rock, hide yourself in the dug-out ground from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty. I indeed exhorted the people, saying, House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. …
2:11:
Here he takes away from them confidence in their own power, and concerning this, he does two things: first, he excludes the power of resistance; second, he rejects the precaution of hiding, where it says, "and they shall go into the holes of rocks" (Isa 2:19).

He sets out two things to exclude the power of resistance. …

The lofty eyes of man are humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. When the enemies have come, and the Babylonian or Roman sword has laid waste the whole province, and the columns of warriors have besieged Jerusalem, then neither riches nor nobility of birth nor the power of offices will be able to defend anyone; but there will be one captivity for all, and God alone will be exalted, whose wrath no one will be able to avoid. …
2:12:
Here is set out the manner of fulfillment of the things that have been predicted. And first, as to the lowering of men; second, as to the subtraction of things, where it says, "and upon all" (Isa 2:13).

Thus he says first: therefore this will be which was said, because "the day of the Lord," that is, the time of vengeance, below: "the day of vengeance is in my heart, the year of my redemption is come" (Isa 63:4); "of hosts," that there be no doubt about victory of him, under whom there is such a multitude of …

For the day of the Lord of hosts is upon everyone proud and lofty, and upon everyone arrogant. These things too are joined to the former. In that day, he says, in which the Lord alone will be exalted, that is, in the day of the Lord's vengeance, all the lofty and the arrogant and the high will be subjected to captivity and the sword. Μεταφορικῶς the word is about the great and the princes: that the more they have been proud, the more they are brought low. …
2:13: Here he places the subtraction of things which make for defense. And first, as to things that pertain to preparing machines of war: either because of their height, and thus he says, "upon all the cedars"; or because of their strength, and thus he says, "upon all the oaks": "open your gates, O Libanus, and let fire devour your cedars" (Zech 11:1); and below this: "howl, you oaks of Basan, because the fenced forest is cut down" (Zech 11:2).

And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan. In Psalm 28 (29) too it is sung: The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and will crush them like the calf of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5, 6). And in Psalm 36 (37): I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found (Ps 36 [37]:35, 36). …
2:14: As to things which pertain to the fortification of places from nature: "and upon all the high mountains": "thus says the Lord God to the mountains, and to the hills, and to the rocks, and the valleys" (Ezek 6:3).

And upon all the lofty mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up. Just as in a good sense, according to the variety of virtues, men are called mountains and hills, so among the impious, according to the diversity of vices, and above all of pride, some are mountains, others hills, upon which the day of the Lord will be; of whom it is written in Ezekiel: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the mountains and the hills: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and your high places shall be scattered, and your altars …
2:15: As to things which pertain to the fortification of places from art: "and upon every high tower": "a day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high bulwarks. And I will distress men" (Zeph 1:16–17).

And upon every lofty tower, and upon every fortified wall. Those who refer these things to the times of Vespasian and Hadrian say that what is written was fulfilled bodily: that no lofty tower, no strongest wall, no multitude of ships and industry of trade could prevail against the might of the Roman army; but that the inhabitants of Judea came into such terror that they, with their wives and children, buried themselves in pits of the earth with the gold and silver which they thought would be a help to them, and …
2:16:
As to things which pertain to abundance of provisions, and thus he says: "and upon all the ships," in which provisions are borne, "of Tharsis," that is, of the sea, below: "howl, you ships of the sea, for the house is destroyed, from whence they were wont to come" (Isa 23:1).

"And upon all that is fair to behold": this pertains to the placating of enemies, or the increase of fighters: "who can despise the people of the Hebrews, who have such beautiful women?" (Jdt 10:18).

And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all that is beautiful to see. For Tarshish, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone translated sea. The Hebrews think that in their own tongue the sea is properly called THARSIS (תרסים), and that when it is called IAM (ים), it is called so not in the Hebrew tongue but in the Syriac. Jehoshaphat too had ships which he sent to Tarshish (1 Kgs 22:49), but they were broken at Ezion-geber. …
2:17: Here it is as if he concludes the proposition; and it is entirely the same as what was said before, except that something is added about the destruction of idols, so that he alone may be shown to be the highest.

And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the height of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day, and the idols shall be utterly broken. Human speech seems to have reason so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood draws near to the truth, like stubble to fire, it is quickly devoured and perishes, and all the doctrines of falsehood, which are now called idols because they are feigned and fabricated, will be utterly broken.
2:18: "And idols shall be utterly destroyed": "your idols shall be broken in pieces and shall be no more, and your temples shall be destroyed" (Ezek 6:6).
2:19: Here he places the precaution of hiding; and it is the same as before, except that here it is foretold as in the future, because he had also explained by foretelling and not by calling down that their power was to be thrown down; "they shall go into the lower parts of the earth: they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword, they shall be the portions of foxes" (Ps 63:9–10).
2:20: Here he removes the third, namely confidence in idols. And first, he takes away their help; "to adore": "And I went in and saw, and behold every form of creeping things, and of living creatures, the abominations, and all the idols of the house of Israel, were painted" (Ezek 8:10). Below: "in that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your hands have made for you to sin" (Isa 31:7).

In that day man shall cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he had made for himself, to worship moles and bats; and he shall go into the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth. …
2:21: Second, he returns to the protection of hiding, where it says, "and he shall go into the clefts of rocks": "every bondman and every freeman hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of mountains" (Rev 6:15).

And when these have been abandoned in the day of the Lord, those who have cast them away will enter the clefts of the rocks and the caverns of the stones, so as to dwell not in the dust of the earth and in vile mud but in firm reason, and find for themselves the various openings of the virtues, through which they may be able to come to the truth. …
2:22:
Here he places sound counsel for escape; therefore since all these things do not avail you, "cease therefore from the man," that is, cease from what is offensive to him, namely Christ, "whose breath is in his nostrils," that is, who breathes with his nostrils and lives like other men as to his humanity; "for he is reputed high," as to his divinity, by the saints and angels: "the Lord is high above all nations; and his glory above all the heavens" (Ps 113:4).

 …

Cease, therefore, from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he himself is reckoned lofty. The Seventy omitted this, and in the Greek copies it was added by Origen under asterisks from the edition of Aquila; in the Hebrew it reads thus: HEDALU LACHEM MEN AADAM ASER NASAMA BAAPHPHO CHI BAMA NESAB HU. Where we have said, he himself is reckoned lofty, Aquila translated, in what is this one reckoned. …
2:6:
Here he shows their guilt. And first, in general, second, in particular, at: "and have had soothsayers."

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he shows their separation from God, when he says, "for you have cast off," and, as the Gloss continues, rightly are they to be called, because you have cast off. "Why are they cast out, he and his seed, and are cast into a land which they know not?" (Jer 22:28). …

Because they have been filled of old, and have had soothsayers, like the Philistines. For Philistines the Seventy always translated foreigners, a common noun for a proper one: this is today the nation of the Palestinians, as it were of the Philisthinians, because the Hebrew tongue does not have the letter P, but uses the Greek PHI in its place. …
2:8:
Here he denounces in them the worship of idolatry; and he adds to the weight of this from three things.

First, from its multitude, where he says, "also is full": "Ephraim has made many altars to sin" (Hos 7:11); "under every green tree, and on every high hill you didst prostitute yourself" (Jer 2:20).

 …

And its land is filled with idols; they have worshiped the work of their own hands, what their fingers have made; and man has bowed himself down, and the man has been humbled. Where once was the Temple and the worship of God, there the statue of Hadrian and the idol of Jupiter were set up. Which many interpret of that testimony which we read in the Gospel: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place (Mark 13:14). …
2:9:
Third, from the dignity of man: and therefore he says: "man," who was made to the image of God, "has bowed himself down," in putting himself under idols; "man," who seems powerful as to acquired things, "has been debased": "man when he was in honor did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts, and is become like to them" (Ps 49:12). Below: "he bows down before it, and adores it, and prays unto it, saying: deliver me" (Isa 44:17).

"Therefore forgive them not." Here he threatens them with punishment. …

Do not, therefore, forgive them. For which the Seventy translated: And I will not forgive them. If God is speaking, it is to be understood thus: Because they have done such things, I will not spare them, nor will I forgive such innumerable sins. If the Prophet, it is to be taken thus: Do not, therefore, forgive those who have committed such crimes. …
30:11: Turn away, inasmuch as they prohibited the word of divine knowledge: who have said to God: depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of your ways (Job 21:14).
30:12: 674. Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel. Here he threatens destruction to them, resuming the subject of their guilt that the punishment may appear more just: because you have rejected this word.

Therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel: Because you have rejected this word, and have hoped in false accusation and tumult, and have leaned upon it: therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach that falls, and is sought for in a high wall: since suddenly, when it is not hoped for, its crushing shall come. …
30:13: And he adds the punishment, where it says, therefore shall this iniquity be to you, signifying sudden punishment by the likeness of ruin, which lies hidden for a long time in a wall that falls suddenly in the end: for the destruction thereof shall come on a sudden: for when they shall say: peace and security; then shall sudden destruction come upon them (1 Thess 5:3).
30:14: And he shows the strong punishment: and it shall be broken small, under the likeness of the breaking of a vessel, of which no fragment remains whole for any use, namely, for carrying fire and drawing water, above: with breaking shall the earth be broken (Isa 24:19).
30:15:
676. For thus says the Lord. Here he denounces their contempt of divine counsel, and concerning this, he sets out three things.

First, the counsel: if you return, below: be converted to me, and you shall be saved (Isa 45:22).

It is never too late to repent. You may have gone down from Jerusalem and may have been wounded on the way; yet the Samaritan will set you upon his beast and will bring you to the inn and will take care of you. The Lord will go forth as a mighty one, as a man of war he will stir up zeal; he will shout and cry aloud; he will prevail over his enemies. …
42:11: Or because their way of life is in the desert: let the desert, that is, its inhabitants, especially as to the Ishmaelites, raise, its voice in praise of God; Cedar, the son of Ishmael, shall dwell in houses, according to the custom of other nations, for they were formerly wanderers through the desert, above: the land that was desolate and impassable shall be glad, and the wilderness shall rejoice (Isa 35:1); or because their habitation is in the mountains: give praise, you inhabitants of Petra, the city in …

Let, he says, the desert and its cities lift up their voice, of which we have also spoken above. Or let the desert rejoice, and its villages, and Kedar, which was once an uninhabitable region beyond Arabia, of the Saracens; and the inhabitants of Petra, which itself is also a city of Palestine. And this signifies that the people of the nations, formerly a desert as regards the knowledge of God and bound by the errors of idolatry, is turned to the praises of the Lord. …
42:12: Second, he foretells the spreading of divine praise: they shall give glory to the Lord, in others, not only in themselves, below: I will send of them that shall be saved, to the Gentiles (Isa 66:19). Mystically, all this refers to the conversion of the gentiles to the faith.
42:13: And the prophetic word describes the glorious coming of the Savior, of which the Apostle Paul also speaks: According to the illumination of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4; 2 Tim 1:10); and compares him to a most mighty man, who is about to fight against his adversaries and to stir up zeal. …
42:15: Fourth, he sets out the punishment as to men: I will lay waste the mountains, the great, hills, the middle ranks, grass, the common people: and I will make mount Seir waste and desolate (Ezek 35:7); and as to the removal of every teaching or consolation, I will turn rivers into islands: he has turned rivers into a wilderness: and the sources of waters into dry ground (Ps 106[107]:33). This can also be referred to the destruction of the enemies of the Jews by Darius.
42:16: And I will lead the blind by the way which before they did not know, of whom we also read above: I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind. These will be led by the way of which Christ speaks: I am the way, or by the way of the knowledge of God; and I will make them walk by the paths of the Prophets. …
42:17: But while I say these things, the people of the Jews has turned back, so as not to believe him who promises, and to be confounded in its errors, and to neglect the pledge of God, having before believed in idols. Or, when the fullness of the nations has come in, then the people of Israel too will be converted (Rom 11), and will repent of its error, through which it had before served idols. …
42:18:
826. Hear, you deaf. Here he shows that they are hard-hearted or disobedient toward his precepts.

And first, he shows their hard-heartedness, calling them deaf and blind unitedly: for their own malice blinded them (Wis 2:21), though they may have the eyes and ears of the body, which shows that those who see take heed and those who have the ears of their hearts open obey.

You deaf, hear, and you blind, look, that you may see. Who is blind but my servant? and deaf but he to whom I have sent my messengers? Who is blind but he who has been sold? and who is blind but the servant of the Lord? You who see many things, will you not keep them? you who have open ears, will you not hear? And the Lord willed to sanctify him, and to magnify the law and exalt it. …
42:19: He that is sold, as a slave of sin for love of temporal good: you are sold, to do evil in the sight of the Lord (1 Kgs 21:20).
42:2:
To which he joins his meekness: he shall not cry: the words of the wise are heard in silence, more than the cry of a prince among fools (Eccl 9:17).

Second, he shows the equality of the judge: nor have respect to person: God is not a respecter of persons (Acts 10:34); to which he joins his piety in coming to help: neither shall his voice, the voice of his preaching, be heard abroad, outside Judea, so that he should first come to the aid of those to whom he was sent (Matt 15:24): to day if you shall hear his …

He will not cry out: for he will be gentle and meek; and he will not accept a person in judgment, or he will not lift up (it is understood) his voice on high. Or, according to Symmachus, he will not be deceived, understanding all the snares of the devil; or, according to the Seventy, he will not let go, namely the people of the Jews, calling them to repentance. Nor will his voice be heard outside: for he did not preach the Gospel outside Galilee and Judea among the other nations. …
42:20: You that have ears open: hear, O foolish people, and without understanding: who have eyes, and see not: and ears, and hear not (Jer 5:21); above: blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy (Isa 6:10).

To him it is said: O Israel, you who see many things, and have very many Prophets through whom to know the commandments of God, will you not keep what has been commanded you? You who have open ears, will you not hear what is said? Of whom we also read above: Hearing you will hear, and will not understand; and seeing you will look, and will not see; for the heart of this people has been made fat (Isa 6:9).
42:21: Second, he shows the foolishness of the hard-hearted, because the Lord intended what is found in the precepts for their own advantage. Hence he sets out the intention of the Lord: and the Lord was willing to sanctify him, the people, both that the people themselves should magnify the law of God in their hearts by keeping it, and that the Lord should exalt the people: for this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3).
The Lord, he says, willed to sanctify him, and to magnify his Law, and to exalt and raise up the people lying prostrate.
42:22: And he also shows their contradiction, because they sinned against themselves: but this is a people that is robbed, by demons through various sins, and therefore they are wasted, by enemies, above: from a people rent and torn in pieces (Isa 18:7); also by others who furnished the occasion of sin: the snare, that is, the occasion of sin, of young men, the foolish: you have been a snare to them (Hos 5:1); and because they hid their sins in the houses of prisons, that is, in the secret of their hearts: with a double …

But he refused to do the will of God, and therefore he was plundered and laid waste by his adversaries, whom we ought to understand either as demons or as enemies. All are the snare of young men, and they are hidden in prison houses. …
42:23:
827. Who is there among you. Here he shows that they cannot be corrected by scourges, because they do not even recognize the cause of the scourges; and concerning this, he does three things.

First, he seeks those who perceive rightly, intimating their scarcity; things to come, which I foretell concerning your punishments: who is wise, and he shall understand these things? (Hos 14:10).

And at the same time the Prophet exhorts them that, if all cannot hear, at least a few may know the things to come and understand from whom they have suffered these things, and may recognize the causes of their devastation, they who would neither hear nor do what had been commanded in the Law.
42:24: Second, he determines the truth as to the doer of the punishment: who has given Jacob for a spoil, the Lord kills and makes alive (1 Sam 2:6); as to the fault: has not the Lord himself, against whom we have sinned: and they have not known his justices, nor walked by the ways of God's commandments (Bar 4:13).
42:25:
And as to the punishment, and he has poured out: pour out your indignation upon them (Ps 68:25[69:24]), "pouring out" signifies its abundance.

Third, he excludes knowledge of the truth: and has burnt him, namely, with material fire through the wasting by their enemies, and he knew not, that he was punished by God for his sins: they have not known nor understood (Ps 81[82]:5).

Therefore the Lord poured out upon them all his anger and an indignation full of fury, so that he who before had kept silent would no longer hold his peace, and would chastise them not with words but with punishments and torments; and a most mighty war would seize them, which they could in no way escape, showing the ferocity of the Romans. …
42:3:
And in dissembling: the bruised reed, namely, the kingdom of the Jews, smoking flax, of the priests: that which was broken you have not bound up (Ezek 34:4).

Third, he shows the truth of his judgment: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth: he shall judge the world with justice, and the people with his truth (Ps 95[96]:13).

A bruised reed, or a broken one, he will not break. For he will be easy to appease toward all, and will give pardon to sinners, saying to the woman: Take heart, daughter, your sins are forgiven you (Luke 7:48). And smoking flax, or, as the others translated, dim and dark, he will not quench: those who were near to being quenched were preserved by the clemency of the Lord (which we have discussed in the works mentioned above concerning the Jews and the nations); but he will judge all things with truth, in no way …
42:4:
To which he joins his pleasantness: he shall not be sad, in his heart, nor troublesome, in his face, for he was always cheerful and pleasant, keeping evenness of mind, even if, as to the sensible part, there was the suffering of sadness, not indeed of necessity, but of will; thus, my soul is sorrowful even unto death (Matt 26:38); the joyfulness of the heart (Sir 30:23[22]).

820. …

But what follows, He will shine and will not be broken, until he sets judgment upon the earth, the Evangelist Matthew did not set down (Matt 12); or else the words in the middle, between judgment and judgment, were removed by a scribe's error. …
42:5:
821. Thus says the Lord God. Here he foretells the sending.

And first, he sets out the power of the one who sends as to the creation of heavenly things: that created the heavens; as to the disposition of earthly things: that established the earth; as to the animation of living things: that gives breath, of natural life, and spirit, freely: the Lord, who stretches forth the heavens, and lays the foundations of the earth, and forms the spirit of man in him (Zech 12:1).

Thus says the Lord God, who creates the heavens and stretches them out, who makes firm the earth and the things that spring from it, who gives breath to the people that is upon it, and spirit to those who tread on it: I the Lord have called you in righteousness, and have taken hold of your hand, and have kept you, and have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you might open the eyes of the blind, and bring the bound out of confinement, out of the prison house those who sit in …
42:6: Second, he foretells the sending, setting out the exaltation of the one sent: I the Lord have called you, my Son, from eternity predestining to the unity of the divine person, in justice, that is, that I may be just, fulfilling my promise: who was predestined the Son of God (Rom 1:4); and taken you by the hand, as to his working: the Father who abides in me, he doth the works (John 14:10), and preserved you, lest you be detained by death: nor will you give your holy one to see corruption (Ps 15[16]:10), below: I …

He, then, whose praises are so great, spoke these things to him whose law the islands and the nations await: I the Lord have called you in righteousness: of whom he himself speaks in the Gospel: Righteous Father, the world does not know you (John 17:25); so that he might be the God not only of the Jews but also of the nations. And I have taken hold of your hand, because whatever the Son works, the Father works. And I have kept you, you who yourself preserve all things. …
42:7: He also shows the use of his office against faithlessness: that you might open the eyes of the blind: for judgment I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind (John 9:39); against the slavery of sin: and bring forth the prisoner out of prison: you also by the blood of your testament have sent forth your prisoners out of the pit (Zech 9:11).
42:8: Third, from the sending he deduces the singularity of the divine majesty as to power: I the Lord: make a way for him who ascends upon the west: the Lord is his name (Ps 67:5[68:4]); my name Adonai (Exod 6:3); my glory, by which I am called Lord: glory to God in the highest (Luke 2:14).

And what he adds, I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another, does not exclude the Son; for when he says in the Gospel, Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was (John 17:5), the Father himself answered: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. …
42:9: And as to knowledge: the things that were first, etc., below: I foretold you of old (Isa 48:5). They also refer this to Darius.

There follows: The former things, behold, they have come. And the sense is: What I have spoken, what I have promised through Moses and the Prophets, all has been fulfilled. But now I announce to you the Gospel, the calling of the nations, the passion of Christ, the newness of faith: so that as you see the former things fulfilled in fact, so you may also believe that the things I now promise will come,
43:1:
And now thus says the Lord. Here he shows them divine love through the remedies which he granted them among their difficulties. And it is divided into three parts: in the first, he promises future remedies to show them his love; in the second, he recalls past benefits to confirm the promise: thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea (Isa 43:16); in the third, he excludes their merits to take away their presumption: but you have not called upon me (Isa 43:22).

 …

And now thus says the Lord who creates you, Jacob, and forms you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you, and I have called you by your name: you are mine. When you pass through the water , I will be with you, and the rivers will not cover you. When you walk into the fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not burn in you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I have given Egypt as your propitiation, Ethiopia and Saba for you. …
43:11: And that he alone is Lord: I am, singularly, I am, preeminently: neither is there salvation in any other (Acts 4:12).

And what follows, And besides me there is no Savior, shows that the Son saves all things in the Father. Of him the same prophet testifies: And the Lord will send them a Savior, who will save them (Isa 19). For God, who is wise and strong, cannot be without his own wisdom and power.
43:12:
Second, he gives a sign of his divinity: I have declared, there was no strange one among you, by which you could know: O Israel, if you will hearken to me, there shall be no new god in you: neither shall you adore a strange god (Ps 81:8–9).

Here he shows the truth of his divinity as to power. And first, he gives the testimony: you are my witnesses: I am the beginning (John 8:25).

Since, then, I foretold from the beginning that these things would come, there will be no one who can refuse my will, nor indeed make void what I shall have done. These things are said indeed to Jacob and Israel, but they refer to the apostolic choir and to all of the people of the Jews who have been willing to believe in Christ.
43:13: He gives a sign of his power in punishing: and there is none that can deliver out of my hand, as in Deuteronomy 32:39 and Job 10:7; and in working: I will work, above: the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who can disannul it? (Isa 14:27).
43:14: Thus says the Lord. Here he sets out the sign of his love, that he destroyed for them the Babylonians, who gloried in their ships because of the multitude of their waters: I sent, namely, my wrath: the Lord has both purposed, and done all that he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon (Jer 51:12).

Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and I have pulled down all the bars, and the Chaldeans glorying in their ships. I am the Lord, your Holy One, the Creator, Israel, your King. LXX: Thus says the Lord God, who redeemed you, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon, and I will rouse up all the fugitives, and the Chaldeans will be bound in ships. I am the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who have shown Israel your king. …
43:16: Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea. Here he recalls his past benefits to confirm their hope for future benefits. And concerning this, he does two things. First, he recalls his past benefits in directing them when they came out of Egypt: in the Red sea (Exod 14); in the mighty waters, in the Arnon (Num 21), in the Jordan (Josh 3).

Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea, and a path in the rushing waters; who brought forth the chariot and the horse, the army and the strong man: together they have fallen asleep, and they will not rise again; they are crushed like flax, they are quenched. Do not remember the former things, and do not look upon the things of old. Behold, I am doing new things; now they will spring forth; surely you will know them. I will make a way in the desert, and rivers in the trackless land. …
43:17: And as to the destruction of their enemies, who brought forth the chariot, the chariots of Pharaoh: his chosen captains are drowned in the Red Sea (Exod 15:4); as flax, cut down in a moment.
43:18: Second, he promises much greater future benefits. First, he shows the greatness of his future benefits by comparison to the former ones: remember not former things, as if to say: they are not worthy to be kept in memory in comparison with future things: forgetting the things that are behind (Phil 3:13).

Therefore I command you this: that among my signs and wonders, by which Babylon, the mightiest city, was overthrown, and by which a way was opened for my people in the Red Sea and in the Jordan, you should in no way remember the old things, since in the Gospel I am going to do far greater things, in comparison with which past things ought to be passed over in silence. For no longer will I find a way in the Red Sea, but in the desert of the whole world. …
43:19: Because of the newness of these things: behold I do new things, unheard of: behold, I make all things new (Rev 21:5); and because of their determination: I will make a way, for those going to the feasts, in the wilderness, that is, the land of the Jews, which was formerly a desert; rivers, of consolation: he has turned a wilderness into pools of waters (Ps 107:35). …
43:2:
He sets out the promise: when you shall pass through the waters, the Egyptians; the rivers, the Chaldeans; the fire, the Greeks; the flames, the Romans: for they were not entirely consumed: we have passed through fire and water (Ps 66:12).

 …

And what he adds, waters and rivers, and fire and flames, describes the onslaught and fury of the persecutors, who begrudge the salvation of the nations and do not want the word of the Gospel to be preached. The Jews, however, would have the Egyptians understood by the waters, the Babylonians by the rivers, the Macedonians by the fire, the Romans by the flame.
43:20: Second, he shows the usefulness of these benefits for the gentiles: the beast of the field shall glorify me, that is, the gentile, living like a beast, converted to Christ, or seeing how I liberated the Jews: beasts and all cattle: serpents and feathered fowls (Ps 148:10); and for the Jews: to give drink, of teaching and consolation: the Lord your God has chosen you (Deut 7:6).

Then what never was done will be done: all the beasts and dragons and ostriches that dwelt in the wilderness of the nations, and were like beasts in the blood of idolatry and the savagery of their manners, will glorify me and praise me together. For dragons, which Theodotion alone, as it is written in the Hebrew, called THANNIM (תנים), the others translated Sirens: monstrous creatures which by their sweet and deadly song cast sailors headlong to be torn apart by Scylla's dogs. …
43:21: Third, he assigns the reason: this people have I formed for myself, namely, for my praise: the Lord has made all things for himself (Prov 16:4).
43:22:
But you have not called upon me. Here he excludes the merits of the Jews for attaining such benefits. And concerning this, he does three things: first, he excludes their merit; second, he gives a place for a response: put me in remembrance (Isa 43:26); third, he removes a certain way of responding: your first father (Isa 43:27).

 …

You have not called upon me, Jacob, nor have you labored in me, Israel. You have not offered me the ram of your burnt offering, and with your victims you have not glorified me. I have not made you serve with offering, nor have I given you labor with incense. You have not bought me sweet cane with silver, and with the fat of your victims you have not made me drunk. But you have made me serve in your sins; you have given me labor in your iniquities. …
43:24: Second, he shows their guilt: but you have made me to serve with your sins, as if to say: you showed me to be servile when you offended me and I did not punish you, above: they are become troublesome to me, I am weary of bearing them (Isa 1:14); he speaks in a human manner.
43:27: Your first father sinned. Here he removes a certain way of responding. For they could allege the innocence of their fathers; but against this, he says, your first father, Adam (Gen 3), Abraham, asking for a sign of the promise of God, as though doubting (Gen 15:8); your teachers, Moses and Aaron at the waters of contradiction (Num 20).

And that you may know that I have mercy on you not for your merit but for my own clemency, I will go back to your fathers and forebears, so that you may understand that you were begotten of sinners: Your first father sinned in the wilderness, namely the whole people of Israel. Or else the author of your race, Abraham, is convicted of having sinned when, as the Lord promised the land of promise to his seed, he answered: Whereby shall I know that I shall possess it? …
43:28: And I have profaned the holy princes, that is, I have allowed them to be profaned; I have given Jacob to slaughter, for they all died in the desert, except for Caleb and Joshua: we have sinned with our fathers (Ps 106:6).
43:3:
And he assigns the reason for this: for I am the Lord, above: for God himself is my savior (Isa 12:2).

Second, he promises the commutation of their punishments, namely, that he would punish others in their place; and he sets out the commutation: I have given Egypt for your atonement, that is, that I may be propitiated toward you, as though by the punishments of those who provoked you to sin by hoping in their help: Saba, a city of Ethiopia: the just is delivered out of distress: and the wicked shall be given up …

And he commands them not to fear for this reason, that the Lord God, their Savior and the Holy One of Israel, is with them, who has made them preach to Egypt, Ethiopia and Syene, and to the furthest bounds of the world. For Syene the other translators put SABA (סבא), whence came the queen of the South, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kgs 10).
43:4: And he assigns the reason, namely, the love of God itself: since you became honorable, that is, I made and reckoned you honorable; I will give men for you, for your liberation: surely Ephraim is an honorable son to me (Jer 31:20).

Therefore the choir of the Apostles has become honorable in the sight of God and beloved by him; and the salvation of all the men and peoples who have been called through them to the Gospel will also be reckoned to the salvation of their own souls.
43:5: Third, he promises them every kind of liberation from tribulation. First, he promises the benefit of liberation: fear not; from the east, for they had been dispersed in every direction, above: he shall assemble the fugitives of Israel (Isa 11:12); behold I will bring them from the north country (Jer 31:8).

Hence he adds and says: Do not fear, I am with you, I who say to you in the Gospel: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age (Matt 28:20). For from the East and from the West I will bring your sons, to rest in the bosom of Abraham; and from all parts of the world a people of my sons and daughters will be gathered, who either call upon my name or are called by my name, so that they are called Christians, to the glory of their founder.
43:7: Second, he sets out their fitness for liberation: and every one that calls upon my name, I will lead into my glory, that he might glorify me, and that I might appear glorious in him: every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved (Joel 2:32).
43:8: Third, he promulgates the command of liberation: bring, O Cyrus, forth, out of the land of their captivity, the people, namely, of the Jews: hear, O foolish people, and without understanding: who have eyes, and see not: and ears, and hear not (Jer 5:21).

And what follows, Bring forth the people that is blind and has eyes, that is deaf and has ears, many think is said of the people of the nations, who through the teaching of the Apostles began to hear and to see. But let us understand this too of scattered Israel, which was called through the Apostles and believed first; to whom Paul also says: It was necessary that the word of God be preached first to you (Acts 13:46). And the Lord himself in the Gospel: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:6). …
43:9: All the nations. Here he excludes the sharing of divinity. And first, he shows the falsehood of other gods by the manner of a judgment, setting out the consensus of the nations in idolatry: assembled together, in one error: they are all gone aside (Ps 14:3); seeking a sign of divinity: who among you, that is, which of your gods; or this is said to the idols; and he seeks testimony: let them bring forth their witnesses, let them be justified, that is, let them justly be called gods; and let the witnesses hear, …
44:1:
And now hear, O Jacob. Here, third, he strengthens them from the worthlessness of the idols, lest perhaps they should believe that the divine promises could be impeded by them. And this is divided into two parts: in the first, he excludes fear; in the second, he shows the worthlessness of the idols, where it says, thus says the Lord the king (Isa 44:6).

Concerning the first, he does three things. …

And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel, whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord, who makes you and forms you from the womb, your helper: Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and you, Most Upright, whom I have chosen. For I will pour out waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground; I will pour out my spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring. And they will spring up among the grass, like willows beside flowing waters. …
44:10:
Who has formed. Here he shows from their formation that they are not gods. And concerning this, he does two things: first, he sets out their formation to exclude their divinity; second, the manner of their formation to show their worthlessness: the smith (Isa 44:12).

Concerning the first, he does two things. First, he sets out their formation, intending this reasoning: what it is made by man is not God, etc. …
44:11: Second, he foretells the confusion of the workers: behold, all the partakers, of the worship of idols, when they come to judgment, shall stand, as if to be judged; the makers are from men, that is, from the number of men: let them be all confounded that adore graven things (Ps 96[97]:7).
44:12: The smith. Here he shows their worthlessness, that not only are they not gods, but even worthless things. And first, he sets out the manner of their formation as to idols made from metal: with the strength of his arm, that is, striking strong blows; he shall hunger and faint, as if to say: the god which he is making cannot help him, although it is especially bound to its maker, above: the coppersmith striking with the hammer (Isa 41:7).

For who could believe that a god is formed by adze, file and auger and hammer? And that images are either cast in the coals, or by rule, plane and corner tools and compass suddenly rise up into gods? Especially since the cheapness of the art is shown by the hunger and thirst of the craftsman. For a wooden statue is made, expressing the human form, and the more beautiful it is, the more august a god it is thought. …
44:13: Second, as to idols which are made from wood: the carpenter. And first, he shows the worthlessness of the idol, setting out its efficient cause with his tools: his rule, for making the wood straight; a plane, an instrument curved back from the side for hollowing out wood; with corners, that is, four-sided in shape, or this is the name of a tool for making shapes of this kind; the compass, that is, the lathe; as to its formal cause: and he has made the image.
44:14: As to its material cause: he has cut down cedars, which are also used for base purposes: the works of the hand of the workman has cut a tree out of the forest (Jer 10:3).
44:18: Second, he shows the blindness of the craftsman: they have not known. Part thereof, of the wood from which the idol was made, now is ashes, for it was burned. Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand, that is, in my working: he is not ashamed to speak to that which has no life (Wis 13:17).

Nor does he understand or consider, nay, he does not see with the eyes either of the flesh or of the mind, that that cannot be God of which a part has been burned in the fire, nor can the divine majesty be made by the hand of a man.
44:2:
846. And now hear, O Jacob. Here, third, he strengthens them from the worthlessness of the idols, lest perhaps they should believe that the divine promises could be impeded by them. And this is divided into two parts: in the first, he excludes fear; in the second, he shows the worthlessness of the idols, where it says, thus says the Lord the king (Isa 44:6).

847. Concerning the first, he does three things. …

Thus says the Lord, your maker and former, who helped you from the womb (Gen 25), so that while still in your mother's womb you seized your brother's heel; or who at the beginning of the newborn Church preserved you from the persecutors. Do not fear their cruelty, Jacob my servant, and Most Upright, whom I have chosen. …
44:21: Remember these things. Here he calls them back to worship of him. And first, he assigns the reason, setting out the duty of servitude: remember these things, that is, consider the worthlessness of idols; my servant: the portion of Jacob is not like them: for he that made all things he it is, and Israel is the scepter of his inheritance (Jer 51:19).

Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are my servant; I have formed you, you are my servant, Israel; do not forget me. I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you.
